title: Interchange (road) - Wikipedia
content: # Interchange (road). In the field of road transport, an **interchange** (American English) or a **grade-separated junction** (British English) is a road junction that uses grade separations to allow for the movement of traffic between two or more roadways or highways, using a system of interconnecting roadways to permit traffic on at least one of the routes to pass through the junction without interruption from crossing traffic streams. Interchanges are almost always used when at least one road is a controlled-access highway (freeway) or a limited-access highway (expressway), though they are sometimes used at junctions between surface streets. *Note:* The descriptions of interchanges apply to countries where vehicles drive on the right side of the road. A cloverleaf interchange is a four-legged junction where left turns across opposing traffic are handled by non-directional loop ramps. A stack interchange is a four-way interchange whereby a semi-directional left turn and a directional right turn are both available.

title: Decode the interstates: What highway numbers actually mean – Greater Greater Washington
content: Why is I-95 named I-95? There’s a logical system behind it all, and it’s easy to learn. One and two-digit interstates span multiple regions, while three-digit interstates are more local. **The one/two-digit system**. There are three factors that go into determining the number for a two-digit interstate:. 2. The lowest numbers begin in the south and west, and get higher as you progressively move north and east. Thus, for example, the name I-95 was reserved for the farthest east major national cross-country interstate that traverses a north-south route. Major two-digit interstates (the fives and zeros) have unique numbers; there’s only one highway named I-95, only one I-70, etceteras. There are a few very short two-digit interstates that probably should have gotten three-digit numbers instead. For example, I-395 connects to I-95, and I-270 connects to I-70. Maryland’s I-270 is a particular troublemaker: Why should a spur connecting to I-70 at only one location get an even first digit instead of an odd?
